subject: Software Craft
title: Clean Architecture
subtitle: A Craftsman Guide to Software Structure
author: Academic Faculty & Domain Curators

pages.title: What Is Software Architecture?
bulletPoints: Architecture is the shape given to a software system by those who build it.
The primary purpose of architecture is to minimize the human resources required to build and maintain the required system.
Behavior vs Structure: Delivering features is secondary to maintaining a flexible, changeable software structure.
The cost of poor design: When systems rot, the cost per line of code increases exponentially toward infinity.

pages.title: Paradigms: Structured, Object-Oriented, and Functional
bulletPoints: Structured Programming: Imposes discipline on direct transfer of control (replacing goto with sequence, selection, iteration).
Object-Oriented Programming: Imposes discipline on indirect transfer of control through polymorphic dispatch.
Functional Programming: Imposes discipline on assignment and variable mutation through referential transparency.
Architectural takeaway: Paradigms tell us what NOT to do rather than adding new capabilities.

pages.title: Design Principles: The SOLID Overview
bulletPoints: SOLID principles guide the arrangement of functions and data structures into classes and module boundaries.
Goal: Create software modules that tolerate change, are easy to understand, and serve as components in diverse systems.
SRP (Single Responsibility), OCP (Open-Closed), LSP (Liskov Substitution), ISP (Interface Segregation), DIP (Dependency Inversion).
SOLID applies equally to class design, microservice architectures, and high-level component packaging.

pages.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
bulletPoints: True definition: A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor (user or stakeholder group).
Common misconception: A module should do only one thing (which is the definition of a refactored function, not SRP!).
Symptoms of violation: Divergent changes, merge conflicts between disparate business departments, and accidental coupling.
Solution: Separate business logic (Payroll, Accounting, HR) into distinct classes with clear domain boundaries.

pages.title: Open-Closed Principle (OCP)
bulletPoints: Definition: A software artifact should be open for extension but closed for modification.
Goal: Make the system easy to extend without incurring high impact of change across existing stable modules.
Architectural mechanism: Partitioning systems into components based on why, when, and how frequently they change.
Inverting dependencies: Higher-level policy components must be completely protected from changes in lower-level detail components.

pages.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
bulletPoints: Definition: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering system correctness.
The classic Square-Rectangle problem: Square inheriting from Rectangle breaks area calculations when width and height are mutated.
Behavioral subtyping: Subclasses must fulfill the contracts, pre-conditions, and post-conditions of their parent abstractions.
Architectural impact: Restricting inheritance to true behavioral equivalence prevents fragile conditional cascades.

pages.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
bulletPoints: Definition: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods that they do not use.
Fat interfaces: Monolithic interfaces bundle unrelated behaviors, causing downstream re-compilation and re-testing.
Decoupling through role interfaces: Decomposing bloated interfaces into fine-grained, client-specific contracts.
Language impacts: Dynamic languages vs statically typed compiled binaries and source-level code dependencies.

pages.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
bulletPoints: Definition 1: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.
Definition 2: Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.
Stable software abstractions: Interfaces and abstract classes are far less volatile than concrete implementations.
Abstract Factories: Using factory design patterns to instantiate volatile concrete classes across architectural boundaries.

pages.title: Component Cohesion: REP, CCP, and CRP
bulletPoints: REP (Reuse/Release Equivalence Principle): The granule of reuse is the granule of release.
CCP (Common Closure Principle): Gather together those things that change for the same reasons and at the same times.
CRP (Common Reuse Principle): Don't force users of a component to depend on things they don't need.
The Tension Triangle: Balancing the trade-offs between reusability, maintainability, and release frequency.

pages.title: Component Coupling: ADP, SDP, and SAP
bulletPoints: ADP (Acyclic Dependencies Principle): Allow no cycles in the component dependency graph.
Eliminating cycles: Inverting dependencies using interfaces or extracting new shared foundation components.
SDP (Stable Dependencies Principle): Depend in the direction of stability (stability = difficulty of change).
SAP (Stable Abstractions Principle): A component should be as abstract as it is stable.

pages.title: Measuring Component Stability & Abstraction
bulletPoints: Afferent Couplings (Ca): Number of external classes that depend on classes within this component.
Efferent Couplings (Ce): Number of classes outside this component that classes within this component depend upon.
Instability metric: I = Ce / (Ca + Ce) (0 = maximally stable, 1 = maximally unstable).
The Main Sequence: Plotting Abstractness (A) vs Instability (I); minimizing Distance D from the Main Sequence.

pages.title: What Is Software Architecture? (Deep Dive)
bulletPoints: Architecture is the strategy that isolates high-level policies from low-level operational details.
The primary purpose of architecture is to facilitate development, deployment, operation, and ongoing maintenance.
Leaving options open: A good architect maximizes the number of decisions that can be deferred or postponed.
Deferring decisions: Delaying choices of database engines, web frameworks, and communication protocols.

pages.title: Independence: Decoupling Policies from Mechanisms
bulletPoints: Use Case Decoupling: Systems should be structured around business use cases rather than frameworks or databases.
Horizontal layering: UI layer, Application business rules, Enterprise business rules, Database access.
Vertical slicing: Slicing across layers by use case (e.g. OrderPlacement, InventoryCheck, InvoiceGeneration).
Decoupled deployment: Independent deployment units (JARs, DLLs, Docker containers, microservices).

pages.title: Drawing Boundaries: The Clean Architecture Core
bulletPoints: Software architecture is the art of drawing lines called architectural boundaries between software elements.
Coupling across boundaries: Crossing lines requires dependency inversion interfaces to prevent pollution.
Plugin architecture: Treating business rules as core engines and UI/Databases as pluggable extensions.
Case study: Why FitNesse ran entirely from in-memory wiki mocks before selecting MySQL storage.

pages.title: Policy and Level: The Hierarchy of Abstraction
bulletPoints: The Level of a component: The distance from physical inputs and outputs.
High-level policies: Business rules, encryption policies, domain calculations that dictate company value.
Low-level mechanisms: Reading mouse events, writing SQL queries, rendering HTML DOM elements.
The Golden Rule: Source code dependencies must always point in the direction of higher level policy!

pages.title: Business Rules: Entities & Use Cases
bulletPoints: Critical Business Rules: Rules that make or save money for the business, even if no computer system existed.
Entities: Business objects encapsulating Critical Business Rules (pure domain data structures and methods).
Use Cases: Application-specific business rules that orchestrate data flow to and from Entities.
Request and Response models: Use cases receive input data structures and return output data structures without UI knowledge.

pages.title: The Clean Architecture Diagram
bulletPoints: Concentric rings: Enterprise Business Rules (Entities) -> Application Rules (Use Cases) -> Interface Adapters -> Frameworks.
The Dependency Rule: Source code dependencies must only point inward toward higher-level policies.
Nothing in an inner circle can know anything at all about something in an outer circle.
Data formats across boundaries: Simple, isolated DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) instead of database entity rows or web forms.

pages.title: Presenters, Views & Humble Objects
bulletPoints: The Humble Object Pattern: Separating hard-to-test behaviors from easy-to-test behaviors.
View is humble: Contains no logic, simply displays pre-formatted strings received from a Presenter.
Presenter is testable: Formats raw data (dates, currency, booleans) into user-ready display models without touching UI widgets.
Database Gateways: Interactors call gateway interfaces; SQL/ORM implementations are humble persistence details.

pages.title: Partial Boundaries & Facades
bulletPoints: The cost of full architectural boundaries: Reciprocal boundary interfaces, DTO marshallers, independent deployments.
Skipping full boundaries: When full boundaries are overkill, one-dimensional boundaries preserve future options.
Strategy pattern: Encapsulating swappable algorithms behind interfaces within a single compilation unit.
Facade pattern: Using a simple structural facade to hide complexity while keeping components in one deployment.

pages.title: The Database Is a Detail
bulletPoints: The database is not the architecture: It is a low-level mechanism for persisting and querying data blocks.
Data models vs Entity models: Storing data in relational tables or JSON documents does not dictate application structure.
Inverting database calls: Business logic interacts with repository interfaces, never raw SQL connections.
Swappable storage: The freedom to switch from relational MySQL to document Mongo or in-memory caches without touching business rules.

pages.title: The Web Is a Detail
bulletPoints: The Web is an I/O device: An HTTP delivery mechanism delivering UI strings to browser windows.
Decoupling from web frameworks: Spring, Express, Rails, and Nuxt are implementation details, not the application.
Testing without the web: Complete business use case test suites running in milliseconds without launching web servers.
Command-line and GUI parity: A clean architecture allows invoking the same business use case from CLI, REST API, or GUI.

pages.title: Frameworks Are Details
bulletPoints: Framework asymmetry: Framework authors love you, but they don't know you; their goals diverge from yours.
The risk of marriage: Tying your domain model directly to framework base classes creates deep vendor lock-in.
Keep frameworks at arm's length: Use frameworks as outer-ring tools, never letting them invade core Entities.
Plugin approach: Treat frameworks as external plugins to your system rather than the foundation of your codebase.

pages.title: Testing Architecture & Test Doubles
bulletPoints: Tests are part of the architecture: They participate in system stability and refactoring confidence.
Fragile Test Problem: Tests that know too much about implementation details break whenever internal code changes.
Testing API: Developing an expressive testing API that invokes use cases directly without touching UI or DB layers.
Mocks, stubs, and fakes: Decoupling test execution from slow network dependencies and disk I/O.

pages.title: Package by Feature vs Package by Component
bulletPoints: Package by Layer: Horizontal organization (controllers, services, repositories) creates weak architectural boundaries.
Package by Feature: Vertical grouping around use cases improves cohesion but can blur boundary encapsulation.
Package by Component: Bundle all use-case logic behind a clean public interface, making implementation details package-private.
Compiler enforcement: Using language access modifiers (internal/package-private) to physically prevent architectural leaks.

pages.title: The Architect's Manifesto: Simplicity & Mastery
bulletPoints: Architecture is an ongoing conversation between business priorities and long-term software health.
Technical debt: The silent killer of software development velocity and developer morale.
Discipline over cleverness: Clean code, clear boundaries, and decoupled dependencies ensure software longevity.
The ultimate test of architecture: The ease with which the system can be evolved, refactored, and maintained over decades.
